finding.claim: GET /mirror passes an attacker-controlled url to httpx after a suffix-only hostname check that lacks a label boundary, so hosts like evilexample.com (attacker-registrable) pass and can resolve to internal addresses.
finding.source: Query parameter 'url' at mirror.py:11 (async def mirror(url: str))

trace.note: url taken directly from the query string
check is host.endswith('example.com'), no dot boundary, so evilexample.com passes
original unparsed url passed to c.get; request goes to the named host
only len(r.text) returned, so impact is blind reachability and a length oracle

finding.guards_checked: urlparse hostname check rejects userinfo (example.com@evil.com), fragment and query tricks; scheme effectively limited to http/https by httpx; no port restriction; no resolved-IP or private-range check; httpx does not follow redirects by default and no follow_redirects=True is set; ALLOWED_SUFFIX (line 7) is defined but unused. Possible urlparse vs httpx parser differential (backslash handling) suspected but unverified.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check is mirror.py:13 `host.endswith("example.com")`, a suffix match with no dot boundary, so it does not close the finding. ALLOWED_SUFFIX (line 7) is unused. No exact-membership, anchored, or IP/private-range check exists before the sink at mirror.py:16.
verdict.reason: The url query parameter (mirror.py:11) reaches `c.get(url)` at mirror.py:16 unchanged, and the only gate at mirror.py:13 is a suffix check, so an attacker-registrable host like evilexample.com passes and the server issues the request to a host the attacker controls and can resolve to an internal address; the endpoint is unauthenticated and the trace lines match the candidate's description.
